newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain deficit worse in August but improvement seen.
newsitem.headline: Spain deficit worse in August but improvement seen.

text.p: The Spanish budget deficit worsened in August from July, but analysts said on Wednesday they considered this a seasonal effect and they were still confident the government would reach its own target.
Earlier, the Bank of Spain said that during the first eight months of the year the deficit was nine percent narrower than in the year-ago period.
That represented a deterioration from July and June.
In the first seven months of the year, the deficit narrowed by 18.7 percent over the year-ago period and by 13.1 percent in the first six months of the year.
"This is not worrying: August is always a peculiar month during which the expenses, especially for interest costs are higher," said Antonio Migelanez, economist at BBV in Madrid.
The central government deficit was 1,184 trillion pesetas for the first seven months of the year, while the August cumulative data showed a figure of 1.987.
In other words, the deficit widened by 803 million pesetas in August over July. It also widened by 10 percent against the year-ago month's amount of 727 million pesetas.
"In August it is pretty normal to have less revenue," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
He forecast a 1996 central government deficit of between about 2.650 trillion and 2.570 trillion pesetas which is in line with what the government's aim.
"In the end, we will see a result pretty similar to what they are expecting," he said.

But for the Spanish government, analysts said, a reduction in the central government budget is not as difficult as respecting the target on the public sector budget gap - which is what is assessed for Europe's single currency criteria.

The public sector budget includes, in addition to the central government budget, the expenditures of the social security body, certain public firms and other expenditures at the regional and local level.

"I do not believe they will have success in obtaining a 4.4 percent level for deficit to gross domestic product. A 5.2 pct level seems more likely to me," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist with the Bank of America in Madrid.
"The public sector deficit will somehow come out at around 5.1 percent of GDP while the central government deficit will be around 4.0 pct," said Luca Jellinek, economist at Banque Paribas in London.
The government's full-year 1996 targets for the central government and for the public sector are, respectively, 3.4 percent and 4.4 percent.
